title: 2.9.3 The void * Type and Type Recasting

questions.q: What does the C type `void *` represent?
choices: A generic pointer: a pointer to any type, or to an unspecified type
A pointer that always holds NULL
A pointer to a function that returns nothing
A pointer that can only point to heap memory
questions.explain: `void *` is C's generic pointer type. It can hold the address of any type.

questions.q: Why can the compiler allocate space for a `void *` variable without knowing what type it points to?
choices: Memory addresses are always stored in the same number of bytes on a given system, so every pointer variable is the same size
The compiler delays allocation until the pointer is first assigned
A `void *` variable is always allocated on the heap
The compiler reserves the size of the largest type a program uses
questions.explain: Every pointer stores an address, and addresses take the same number of bytes (for example 4 on 32-bit systems and 8 on 64-bit systems). Because of that, the size of a `void *` is known no matter what it points to.

questions.q: On a 64-bit system, how many bytes of storage does a `void *` variable need?
questions.explain: Addresses are eight bytes on 64-bit systems, and every pointer variable, including `void *`, stores one address.

questions.q: On a 32-bit system, how many bytes of storage does a `void *` variable need?
questions.explain: Addresses are four bytes on 32-bit systems, so every pointer variable takes four bytes.

questions.q: Given `void *gen_ptr; int x; char ch;`, which statements are valid C?
choices: `gen_ptr = &x;`
`gen_ptr = &ch;`
`*gen_ptr = 5;`
`ch = *gen_ptr;`
questions.explain: A `void *` can be assigned the address of any type. It cannot be dereferenced directly, so `*gen_ptr` is invalid on either side of an assignment.

questions.q: A `void *` can be dereferenced directly as long as it holds a valid address.
questions.explain: A `void *` can never be dereferenced directly, because the compiler does not know the size of the memory it points to. You have to recast it to a specific pointer type first.

questions.q: Why does the compiler refuse to dereference a `void *` directly?
choices: It does not know the size of the memory the address points to (for example, a 4-byte int or a 1-byte char)
The address in a `void *` might be on the stack
A `void *` stores half of an address
Dereferencing a `void *` would always produce zero
questions.explain: To dereference a pointer, the compiler has to know how many bytes to access and how to read them. A `void *` gives it no type information, so it cannot generate that code.

questions.q: Before dereferencing a `void *`, the programmer must explicitly ______ it to a pointer of a specific type. (one word)
questions.explain: Recasting (casting) the `void *` tells the compiler which specific pointer type it is.

questions.q: Recasting a `void *` to a specific pointer type tells the compiler the type, so it can generate the correct memory access code when the pointer is dereferenced.
questions.explain: That is the purpose of the recast: once the compiler knows the type, it knows how many bytes to access and how to interpret them.

questions.q: `args` is a `void *` that holds the address of an `int`. Which expression correctly gets the int value?
choices: `*((int *)args)`
`*args`
`(int)*args`
`(int *)*args`
questions.explain: First recast `args` to an `int *`, then dereference it. The other choices all dereference the `void *` before (or without) recasting it.

questions.q: When a function receives a `void *` parameter, the compiler works out what type it really points to and recasts it automatically.
questions.explain: The compiler has no way to know the real type. The programmer knows what type was passed in and must recast the pointer explicitly before dereferencing it.

questions.q: Which of these are common uses of `void *`?
choices: Return type of functions that return newly allocated memory that can store any type, such as `malloc`
Parameter type for functions that can accept a pointer to any type of value
Storing an int or char value directly in the pointer variable instead of an address
Creating a pointer that can be dereferenced without knowing the type it points to
questions.explain: `void *` is mostly used for generic return types (like `malloc`) and generic parameters. It still stores an address, not a value, and it cannot be dereferenced without a recast.

questions.q: What is the return type of `malloc`?
choices: `void *`
`int *`
`char *`
`void`
questions.explain: `malloc` returns a `void *` because the memory it allocates can be used to store any type.

choices: Recasts malloc's `void *` return value to an `int *` to match the type of `array`
Tells malloc to store the value 10 in the new memory
Converts the size argument into a pointer
Dereferences the memory that malloc returned
questions.explain: `malloc` returns a `void *`. The `(int *)` recasts it to the specific pointer type of the variable that stores the heap address.

questions.q: Why does `pthread_create` use a `void *` parameter for the argument it passes to the thread main function?
choices: It makes `pthread_create` generic, so a program can pass a pointer to any application-specific type
Threads can only share data through pointers to char
It stops the thread from reading the argument
It makes the argument be copied onto the heap automatically
questions.explain: Because the parameter is a `void *`, `pthread_create` can accept a pointer to any type of memory location. The thread function then recasts it to the type it knows was passed.

questions.q: In `main`, `x = 6;` and `(void *)(&x)` is passed to `pthread_create` as the argument for the thread function `my_thr_main(void *args)`. Inside `my_thr_main`, `num = *((int *)args);` runs. What value does `num` get?
questions.explain: `args` holds the address of `x`. Recasting it to `int *` and dereferencing it reads the int stored at that address, which is 6.

questions.q: In the call `pthread_create(&tid, NULL, my_thr_main, (void *)(&x));`, why is `&x` written as `(void *)(&x)`?
choices: To recast the `int *` to a `void *` so it matches the type of `pthread_create`'s parameter
To dereference `x` before the thread starts
To make a copy of `x` on the heap
To convert the value of `x` into an address
questions.explain: `&x` has type `int *`. The cast to `(void *)` matches the generic `void *` parameter of `pthread_create`. The address itself does not change.
